subsection: 3. Partition and Northern Ireland under the Unionist Party, 1912–1949

notes.b: Partition (the division of Ireland into Northern Ireland and Southern Ireland) came about because unionists would not accept Home Rule (self-government for Ireland within the United Kingdom), British governments failed to find an all-Ireland settlement, and the 1918 vote showed a divided island.
points: Unionist resistance came first: the Ulster Covenant (signed 28 September 1912) and the Ulster Volunteer Force, or UVF (an armed unionist militia formed in January 1913), showed that Home Rule for all Ireland could be imposed only by force.

Exclusion debates followed, all assuming that some Ulster counties would be left out of Home Rule. These were the county option (Asquith's proposal of March 1914, letting Ulster counties opt out for six years), the failed Buckingham Palace Conference (July 1914) and Lloyd George's 1916 proposals.

The 1916 plan collapsed over whether exclusion would be permanent or temporary: nationalists were told it would be temporary, while unionists were told it would be permanent. Unionist and Conservative members of the cabinet, including Lansdowne and Long, then insisted on permanence.
The First World War and the 1916 Rising changed nationalist politics, and the Irish Convention of 1917–18 failed to produce agreement. Sinn Féin, the rising republican party, boycotted it.
The 1918 general election (December) confirmed the divide, because Sinn Féin won 73 seats, the Irish Parliamentary Party 6, and unionists 26, mostly in the north-east.

The six counties were chosen, not all nine of Ulster. Only Antrim, Down, Armagh and Londonderry had unionist majorities, Tyrone and Fermanagh had narrow nationalist majorities, and Donegal, Cavan and Monaghan were left out. Six counties gave a safer unionist majority than nine would have.

Northern Ireland had about 1.25 million people (1926 census), of whom about two-thirds were Protestant and about one-third Catholic. This one-third minority is why the new state's treatment of Catholics mattered so much later.

British policy made partition the practical answer. Lloyd George's coalition, with a large Conservative element, was unwilling to coerce Ulster, so the Government of Ireland Act of 1920 gave the unionists the offer of their own parliament.
notes.tip: The commonest Higher essay asks for the factors in partition. Name three linked factors (unionist resistance and the threat of force; repeated British failure to find a settlement, with the 1914 and 1916 proposals; the divided 1918 result and the logic of six counties), give dates, and judge which mattered most. Narrating the Home Rule crisis without a judgement scores poorly. If asked why six counties, use the Tyrone and Fermanagh majorities and the safer majority.

notes.h: The Government of Ireland Act and the new state, 1920–1925
notes.b: The Act of 1920 created two Home Rule parliaments, but only the northern one worked. The Treaty then let Northern Ireland stay out of the Free State, and the Boundary Commission failed to move the border.
points: The Government of Ireland Act (royal assent December 1920) set up a parliament for the six counties of Northern Ireland and one for the 26 counties of Southern Ireland. A Council of Ireland was meant to link the two, but it never worked.
In the Northern election of 24 May 1921 the Unionists won 40 of 52 seats. Sinn Féin and the Nationalists won six each but refused to take part, an abstention (staying away from the parliament).
Craig became Prime Minister on 7 June 1921, and George V opened the Northern parliament in Belfast on 22 June 1921, which gave the new state royal approval.

Southern Ireland's parliament never worked, because Sinn Féin won 124 of 128 seats in the same election (the other four went to Dublin University unionists) and treated it as an election to the Dáil, the republican assembly.

Under the Treaty (the 1921 agreement creating the Irish Free State) Northern Ireland could opt out of the Free State. It did so on 7 December 1922, the day after the Free State came into being on 6 December.

The Treaty also provided for a Boundary Commission (set up 1924) to review the border. Richard Feetham, a South African judge, was chair, with Eoin MacNeill for the Free State and J.R. Fisher for Northern Ireland, appointed by Britain because Craig refused to nominate.

The commission's expected report was leaked to the Morning Post in November 1925, and MacNeill resigned. On 3 December 1925 the three governments (British, Free State and Northern Ireland) agreed in the Tripartite Agreement that the border would stay as it was.

The Tripartite Agreement also released the Free State from its share of the imperial (UK) debt and abolished the powers of the Council of Ireland. So the border was fixed, and the Council had no further role.
notes.tip: Keep the dates apart: the 1920 Act had two parliaments, the Treaty (1921) created the Free State, and Northern Ireland opted out on 7 December 1922. The Council of Ireland came from the Act, the Boundary Commission from the Treaty. The report was leaked in November 1925 and the Tripartite Agreement came on 3 December 1925. Be ready to say why the Commission failed to move the border.

notes.b: The new state was born amid sectarian rioting and an IRA campaign. The government answered with a Protestant-recruited police force and exceptional powers that stayed in place long after the crisis.
points: Expulsions of Catholic workers, and of some Protestant labour supporters, from the Belfast shipyards began in July 1920 amid IRA violence and unionist anger. Thousands of people were affected.
Riots in Derry in June 1920 and in Belfast through 1920–22 killed about 500 people, most of them Catholics, and drove many families from their homes.
The Dáil organised a boycott of Belfast goods in 1920. It hurt Catholic workers and shopkeepers in Belfast more than it hurt unionist business.
The Ulster Special Constabulary, formed in late 1920, had full-time A Specials, part-time B Specials and reserve C Specials. It was recruited almost entirely from Protestants.
The Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC) replaced the older Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC) in June 1922. A third of its places were notionally reserved for Catholics, but Catholics never filled them.
The Craig–Collins pacts of January and March 1922 failed. After the IRA offensive on the border in May 1922 the government interned republicans (imprisoned them without trial).

The Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act of April 1922 allowed internment, curfews, the banning of meetings and organisations, and arrest without warrant. It was renewed each year and made permanent in 1933.
Some of the interned men were held on the prison ship Argenta in 1922.
notes.tip: Know the three forces apart: A, B and C Specials (1920), the RUC (1922) and the RIC (the older force). A question may ask why the Special Powers Act was passed (the violence and the border offensive of 1922) and why it was made permanent. Short-answer questions want exact names and dates for the Act.

notes.h: The Unionist government in power: control of the system
notes.b: The Ulster Unionist Party governed without interruption from 1921. It also changed the electoral rules in ways that kept it in power, while nationalists took little part in the system.
points: Nationalists abstained from Stormont (the Northern Ireland parliament, named after its later building) at first. The Nationalist Party under Joe Devlin took its seats in 1925, but Sinn Féin remained abstentionist.

In 1922 Tyrone and Fermanagh county councils, which refused to recognise the Belfast government, were dissolved and replaced by commissioners (officials appointed by the government), as were other nationalist-controlled councils.
The Local Government Act of 1922 abolished proportional representation, or PR (a voting system that gives parties seats in proportion to their votes), in local elections, and boundaries were redrawn.
PR for Stormont elections was abolished in 1929 and replaced by single-member constituencies (one winner per area). This helped the Unionists and hurt Labour and independents.

Derry Corporation stayed under unionist control from 1923 to 1969 although Catholics were a majority of the city's population. This is the best-known case of gerrymandering, drawing electoral boundaries to favour one side.
The Unionist Party won every Stormont election from 1921 to 1969 by large margins. A bloc vote on the border issue kept Protestant workers within the party.

Stormont Parliament Buildings, on the outskirts of Belfast, were opened by the Prince of Wales in 1932. Before then the parliament had sat in the Presbyterian Assembly's College in Belfast, so the new building was a symbol of the permanence of the state.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two abolitions of PR: local elections in 1922 and Stormont in 1929. For a paragraph on how the Unionist Party kept power, give both dates, single-member constituencies, Derry and the unbroken Stormont victories from 1921 to 1969. If asked to explain gerrymandering, use Derry as the example.

notes.h: Discrimination in jobs, housing and public life
notes.b: Discrimination means unequal treatment of Catholics in jobs, housing, policing and local government. Nationalists said that the state practised it, while unionists denied it and argued that Catholics refused to take part in the state.
points: Catholics were about a third of the population but held a small share of senior posts, for example in the civil service, the judiciary and local government.

The shipyards and heavy industry employed few Catholics. Protestant workers' networks and the Orange Order (a Protestant fraternal society) helped to secure jobs for their own members, which kept the pattern in place.
Local councils controlled by unionists allocated public housing, so nationalists argued that houses went to Protestant families first.
In speeches in the 1930s (in 1933 and 1934) Basil Brooke urged unionists not to employ Catholics. His remarks are widely quoted as evidence of the attitudes of leading unionists.

On 24 April 1934 Craig told the Stormont parliament, in reply to claims that the South was a Catholic state, that he boasted of “a Protestant Parliament and a Protestant State”. It is the best-known statement of the attitudes of the unionist government.

Historians disagree. Michael Farrell, in The Orange State (1976), sees systematic discrimination, while others accept discrimination in some fields but stress that it was uneven and not centrally planned.

Unionists defended the system by pointing to nationalist non-participation. Abstention in the early years and the Catholic Church's separate schools left the minority with a limited voice in the state.
notes.tip: Unsupported claims of discrimination earn little, so use specific evidence: the Derry gerrymander, housing, the shipyards, and Brooke's and Craig's speeches. Then show the historians' disagreement (Farrell against those who say it was uneven). Do not confuse Basil Brooke with Dawson Bates, who was Minister of Home Affairs.

notes.h: The economy and society in the North, 1921–1939
notes.b: Northern Ireland began with high-value industries that depended on export markets. The post-war slump and then the Depression hit them hard, so poverty and unemployment shaped the state's first two decades.
points: Shipbuilding at Harland and Wolff and linen were the two main industries. Both fell back after the post-war boom ended in 1920–21, because they depended on export markets.
Unemployment was about 20 per cent for much of the 1920s and above 25 per cent in the early 1930s, among the highest in the United Kingdom.
Agriculture remained important because small farms could still sell goods, such as cattle and eggs, to Britain.

The government followed a policy of ‘step by step’ with Britain, keeping welfare benefits such as pensions and unemployment pay in line with British levels. This was financed by the Imperial Contribution (Northern Ireland's payment towards UK-wide costs).
Housing in the slums of Belfast was poor and overcrowded because the government built little until the late 1930s.

In October 1932 unemployed Catholic and Protestant workers joined together in the Outdoor Relief strike and riots in Belfast against the harsh relief rules (the payments to the unemployed). Police shot dead two people, and relief rates were increased.
notes.tip: The Outdoor Relief riots of October 1932 are good dated evidence in an essay on the economy and unemployment, and they show Catholics and Protestants acting together. In a question on how the government dealt with its challenges, pair the success of parity on welfare with the failure of housing and economic policy.

notes.h: The impact of partition on the island's economy and society
notes.b: Partition broke up an economy that had been built on all-Ireland trade, and it weakened both parts. It also left a lasting political issue in the border.
points: Customs controls on the border from 1923 interrupted the flow of goods and cattle. The Economic War (1932–38) between the Free State and Britain then made smuggling common.
Belfast's linen, shipbuilding and engineering had sold to a UK and world market, so they lost the southern market they had counted on.
The South lost most of the island's large-scale industry, which was in the north-east, so it was left with an economy dependent on agriculture.
Railways were also split by the border. The Great Northern Railway, for example, crossed it.
Society divided as well. Catholics in the North were cut off from the southern state's institutions, while the Southern Protestant minority declined and had a smaller place in public life.
Politically the border became the main theme of Northern nationalism and of southern foreign policy. Articles 2 and 3 of the 1937 Constitution claimed the whole island.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on the economic effects of partition, use four points: border customs controls, the South's dependence on agriculture, Belfast industries cut off from the southern market, and the Economic War.

notes.b: Craig organised unionist resistance to Home Rule and became the first Prime Minister of Northern Ireland. He is judged both as the builder of a stable state and as the leader of a sectarian one.
points: Craig (1871–1940) was born in Belfast, the son of a wealthy whiskey distiller, and worked as a stockbroker. He served in the Boer War and became MP for East Down in 1906.

Before partition he organised the UVF and the Larne gun-running of April 1914 with Carson (the unionist leader). From 1916 to 1921 he held junior ministerial posts in the British government, the last as Parliamentary and Financial Secretary to the Admiralty (1920–21).

He succeeded Carson as Unionist leader in February 1921 and became Prime Minister of Northern Ireland in June 1921, serving until his death on 24 November 1940. He was made Viscount Craigavon in 1927.
He met Collins in January and March 1922 (the pacts) and negotiated with Lloyd George, but insisted that the border was settled. He also refused to nominate a member to the Boundary Commission.

His government created the RUC and the Special Powers Act and abolished PR, and he told Stormont in 1934 that it was a Protestant parliament and state. Critics therefore see him as a sectarian figure. His government also kept welfare in line with Britain's step by step.
Events shaped him: the violence of 1920–22, the Boundary Commission and the Depression all shaped him. His defenders say he held the state together against IRA violence and economic crisis.
Contemporaries: unionists revered him as the founder of their state, while nationalists considered him responsible for their exclusion and for sectarian rule.

Historians: Patrick Buckland's biography James Craig (1980) portrays a cautious, conservative leader who made no attempt to win Catholic consent. Others likewise criticise the lack of any attempt to win minority consent.
notes.tip: In a Higher essay on Craig's strengths and weaknesses, contrast the organiser and builder of a stable state with the leader of a Protestant state who made no outreach to Catholics, and name Buckland for weight. For a 40-mark Ordinary Level paragraph, cover Larne, succession in 1921, the opening of parliament, the Boundary Commission refusal, Viscount Craigavon, death in 1940, and at least one achievement and one criticism.

notes.b: Bates was the minister who ran the machinery of control for more than 20 years. His name is tied to the security system and the electoral changes.
points: Richard Dawson Bates (1876–1949) was a Belfast solicitor. He was secretary of the Ulster Unionist Council (the governing body of the unionist movement) from 1906 to 1921 and helped to organise the UVF.
He was Minister of Home Affairs from 1921 to 1943, which made him responsible for the RUC, the Special Constabulary, the Special Powers Act, local government and elections.
He introduced the Special Powers Act and the Local Government Act of 1922, which abolished PR for local elections, and he was the minister responsible for the 1929 change for Stormont elections.
He used his powers to ban republican parades and organisations, to arrest and intern suspects and to censor some publications.
Events shaped him: the security crisis of 1921–22 created the powers that he then used for over twenty years. He left office in 1943 in ill health.
Contemporaries: nationalists blamed his department for the system of control, and many unionists praised his efficiency.

Historians: Patrick Buckland, in The Factory of Grievances: Devolved Government in Northern Ireland, 1921–39 (1979), describes how his department's decisions, even if cautious, left a legacy of grievances.
notes.tip: For a 30-mark Ordinary Level paragraph on Bates, say who he was (solicitor, Ulster Unionist Council secretary, UVF), his office and dates (Home Affairs 1921–43), what he did (RUC, Special Powers Act, local government and elections), and one judgement. Do not confuse him with Basil Brooke, a different minister who later became Prime Minister.

notes.h: Assessment: the Unionist state's achievements and limits
notes.b: Judgements depend on whether the state is measured by survival and stability or by its treatment of the minority. Good answers set paired points against each other and reach a verdict.
points: Achievement: it survived the violence of 1920–22 and the Depression, and secured the position of Northern Ireland within the United Kingdom.
Achievement: through its step-by-step parity policy it maintained British standards in education, health and welfare.
Limit: it relied on emergency powers, a largely Protestant police and manipulated electoral rules, so the minority never accepted the state.
Limit: a one-party government with a permanent majority did not develop real opposition, and its economic and housing policy was timid.
Contemporary view: unionists regarded the state as a bulwark against a Catholic all-Ireland state, while nationalists saw a Protestant state.
Later view: historians disagree on how far the system was planned discrimination, but accept that its legacy shaped the Troubles.
notes.tip: In an essay on how the Unionist government dealt with its challenges, group evidence under security and violence, the nationalist minority, and the economy and unemployment. Pair success in security and survival with failure in fairness and in economic and housing policy, with dated evidence such as the Special Powers Act, the B Specials, PR abolition, the Outdoor Relief riots and parity.

keyTerms.definition: The division of Ireland under the Government of Ireland Act 1920 into Northern Ireland (six counties) and Southern Ireland.
The movement, led by Carson and Craig, that opposed Home Rule and then defended Northern Ireland's place in the United Kingdom.
The unequal treatment of Catholics in jobs, housing, policing and local government in Northern Ireland, as alleged by nationalists.
The Act that created two parliaments in Ireland and is the legal basis of Northern Ireland.
The commission provided for in the Treaty to decide the border, which in 1925 left the border unchanged.
The 1922 law giving the Northern Ireland government powers of internment, curfew and banning; permanent from 1933.
The part-time police reserve formed in 1920, whose B Specials were almost wholly Protestant.
Drawing electoral boundaries to give one party an unfair advantage, as in Derry's local elections.
An electoral system in which seats match shares of votes; abolished for Northern local elections in 1922 and for Stormont in 1929.
The Northern Ireland parliament, which sat at the Presbyterian Assembly's College in Belfast until Parliament Buildings at Stormont opened in 1932.
